segments.text: A gunner falls out of a burning bomber, four miles above France, with no parachute. Under him is a railway station with a glass roof.
Four miles, onto glass? No chance. Let's go back to the start.
Alan Magee is from New Jersey. He joins up right after Pearl Harbor, and they make him a ball turret gunner: the man in the steel and glass ball under the belly of a B-17.
The ball is so cramped that there is no room to wear a parachute in it. His waits up in the fuselage.

Third of January, {1943|nineteen forty-three}. His seventh mission. His bomber is called Snap! Crackle! Pop!, named by a pilot who used to work for the cereal company. The target is the U-boat base at Saint-Nazaire. In daylight.
Over the target, the flak comes up. One burst wrecks his turret, and wounds him. He hauls himself out, into the fuselage.
And reaches for his parachute. The flak has torn it to rags. I checked it myself. Useless.
Then a second hit takes off part of the right wing. The bomber catches fire, and starts to spin.
Up there, the air is too thin to breathe. Magee blacks out. And the spinning bomber throws him clear.
He falls unconscious. How far? The bomb group's own report says about {20,000|twenty thousand} feet. Later tellings say {22,000|twenty-two thousand}. Either way, call it four miles.
And this is where it stops making sense. Right under him is the railway station of Saint-Nazaire. Its roof is glass, on an iron frame.
He goes straight through it. The glass bursts, and takes some of the speed out of him.
Where he ends up, the accounts don't agree. Some say the station floor. Some say he hung in the steel girders of the roof. They agree on one thing. He is alive.
Only just. Twenty-eight shrapnel wounds. A broken leg and ankle. A punctured lung. And a right arm he is about to lose.
He is a prisoner now, and his doctor is a German. As Magee told it later, the doctor says they are enemies, but that he is a doctor first, and will do his best to save that arm.
He does. Magee keeps the arm, and in time he recovers completely. He never learns the doctor's name.
Ten men were on that bomber. Three lived. Seven did not come home.
The three survivors are sent to a prison camp, Stalag Seventeen B. Magee is there until May {1945|nineteen forty-five}, when the war in Europe ends, and he is free.
He goes home with a Purple Heart and an Air Medal. And then, of all things, the man who fell out of the sky learns to fly. He earns a pilot's licence, and works around aeroplanes.
Fifty years after the raid, the people of Saint-Nazaire put up a memorial to the crew of his bomber. And Alan Magee, with his wife Helen, came back to France to stand in front of it.
He died in {2003|two thousand and three}, in Texas. He was eighty-four.
No parachute. Four miles. One glass roof. I said no chance. I was wrong. Case closed.
